The use of exam wrappers to promote metacognition
Adam Patea,⁎, Elizabeth M. Lafitteb, Sujith Ramachandrana, David J. Caldwellc

A B S T R A C T
Introduction: Self-directed learning, self-awareness, and metacognition are becoming more
heavily emphasized in healthcare education. Metacognitive activities may be used to promote
self-awareness and development of effective self-directed learning strategies. Exam wrappers
(wrappers) are a metacognitive tool utilized in other areas of higher education that offer students
the ability to learn from exam performance by reviewing missed items in a reflective manner.
Wrappers encourage structured reflection and planning for future learning.
Methods: Pharmacy students enrolled in a pathophysiology course were provided structured
exam reviews with an opportunity to utilize a wrapper. A baseline questionnaire was given two
weeks before the first exam to assess baseline characteristics. Wrappers were provided before
Exams 2, 3, 4, and 5, and the effects on exam performance were measured. Mixed effects
modeling was utilized for final analysis of effect on student performance.
Results: Exam wrapper vs. non-wrapper groups were self-selected, with 53 students participating
in at least one wrapper and 35 never utilizing a wrapper. Mixed effects modeling analysis found a
non-significant increase in average exam performance (p = 0.142).
Conclusion: Wrappers have potential as an additional metacognitive tool for exam review.
Further studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and impact more broadly in pharmacy
education.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Lifelong learning, self-directed learning, reflection, and metacognition are terms with which many pharmacy educators are be- coming familiar. The Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE) 2016 Standards emphasize development of self- awareness in students and creation of a culture that promotes self-directed, lifelong learning. 1 Effective metacognition, which is simply “thinking about thinking,” is a critical element for this type of learning to occur. 2 Unfortunately, many students have not utilized the cognitive processes (i.e. metacognition/reflective thinking) necessary for self-directed learning to occur and are com- pletely unfamiliar with evidence-based learning strategies. This makes self-directed learning a challenge. One way that educators can assist students in developing skills for self-directed learning is to facilitate metacognitive practices. Medina et al. 2 provide a detailed and useful review of several strategies to improve student metacognition, including exam review. Exam reviews may offer an especially appealing opportunity for enhancing metacognition due to their position in the current workflow of many courses. Limited published research exists describing exam review practices, but what is available indicates they https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cptl.2019.02.008 ⁎ Corresponding author. T are common, highly variable in format, and a subjectively useful tool for learning that may positively impact student performance. 3–5 Exam reviews may be enhanced by the inclusion of activities that are designed to promote critical self-evaluation of knowledge, skills, and abilities. These activities may help establish and develop habits of reflective thinking and metacognition as part of the study cycle. One academic tool that may accomplish these goals during exam reviews is the “exam wrapper”. Exam wrappers are a metacognitive tool used in conjunction with exam review that guide students to reflect in three key areas: preparation, types of errors made, and what they will change in preparation for the next exam. Although format varies, these tools typically consist of probing questions that guide self-reflection about preparation and performance on the exam, categorizing exam errors by type and frequency, and synthesis of this information to develop goals and strategies to address self-identified strengths and weaknesses. 6 Exam wrappers prompt students to learn from the exam rather than only for the exam and have been used throughout higher education in a number of disciplines. 7–9 Several examples of exam wrapper implementation and assessment are described in the literature, and variable levels of success and failure with respect to impact on metacognition, course performance, and student perception of value have been reported. 10 , 11 Various other metacognitive exercises and their effect on pharmacy student performance/metacognition have been reported in the literature. 12–16 These studies have found that higher achieving students typically display greater self-awareness and metacognition, but none of these articles have directly looked at exam reviews as a metacognitive tool or the effect of this activity. The paucity of literature examining the impact of exam reviews on student outcomes, paired with the greater accreditation emphasis on soft skills, suggests the need for development and evaluation of methods to facilitate metacognitive practices that are critical for students to successfully become self-directed learners. Currently, faculty at the University of Louisiana Monroe offer exam reviews using optional one-on-one office review sessions and in-class exam review. sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This exam wrapper pilot study took place in a first year pathophysiology course at the University of Louisiana Monroe. The course is team-taught by three different faculty members in the school's Department of Basic Pharmaceutical Sciences and has historically been a challenging course for first-year students. The instructors, content, and delivery of material remained unchanged during the exam wrapper intervention. Course performance was evaluated with five multiple choice exams, administered electronically using ExamSoft. Design of the educational activity The research protocol and all research materials were reviewed and approved by the University of Louisiana Monroe Institutional Review Board. The intervention consisted of two parts 1 : a 30-min introduction to metacognition and evidence-based learning stra- tegies presented to all incoming first year students; and 2 a series of structured, voluntary one-hour exam reviews that took place outside of class time at a date and time selected by enrolled students. The introduction to metacognition was presented during pharmacy school orientation one week prior to the beginning of the fall semester. Two schools of pharmacy faculty members with no teaching responsibilities in the pathophysiology course facilitated all structured exam reviews and exam wrapper administration. The first exam review included a brief overview of the exam wrapper activity; teaching faculty in the course were available during all reviews to answer student questions. The structured exam review was conducted four times, once after each exam except the final. During the exam review, students were provided a paper copy of their individualized ExamSoft missed item report and given an opportunity to participate in a voluntary exam wrapper that was administered through Google Forms via a hyperlink in the course management system. Missed item reports were handed out for those who attended the review and collected as documentation of exam review attendance. Time was also allotted and prompts given in exam reviews for peer to peer and group discussion of exam questions and successful study strategies, followed by question-and-answer feedback with teaching faculty in the course. The exam wrapper is shown in Fig. 1 and was adapted from existing examples in the literature and reviewed by five faculty members for face validity. 7–9 Students were also allowed to review exams individually with the instructors represented on the exam outside the structured exam review. No bonus points or other incentives were offered for participation in exam reviews or completion of exam wrappers. Because participation in the exam wrapper was voluntary and independent of taking part in the exam review, the number of students who chose to take the exam wrapper differed for each administration. Evaluation of the educational activity This exam wrapper activity was evaluated with multiple surveys, the exam wrapper responses themselves, and student perfor- mance. An identifiable baseline survey was administered two weeks before the first exam to capture study habits and other char- acteristics before the administration of any exam wrappers and is included in Table 1 . Additionally, a descriptive post-activity survey evaluating the exam wrapper and review process was given at the end of the semester ( Table 2 ). Student performance was evaluated A. Pate, et al. Currents in Pharmacy Teaching and Learning 11 (2019) 492–498 493 using immediate next exam performance post-exam wrapper (i.e. students' Exam 2 performances after taking the Exam 1 exam wrapper). Exam 1 was excluded from measurement because the first opportunity to administer the wrapper occurred after the first exam. Student performance on the first exam was unaffected by the exam wrapper intervention and was used as an indicator of the student's baseline academic ability in the course. sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The overall response rate for the baseline survey was 100% (88/88). Throughout the semester, 53 (60%) students participated in at least one exam wrapper activity and 35 (40%) never participated. Overall, 25 individual students participated in the wrapper after Exam 1, 19 participated after Exam 2, six after Exam 3, and only three students participated in the wrapper after Exam 4. Baseline characteristics for students completing at least one exam wrapper are provided in Table 1 . These include learning strategies, study habits, use of study aids, and pre-pharmacy math/science GPA. The baseline characteristics of students who took the exam wrapper at least once vs. those who did not take any exam wrappers were not significantly different, with the exception of first exam perfor- mance; students who took the exam wrapper at least once scored significantly lower on Exam 1 than students who did not take at least one exam wrapper (84.4% vs. 88.6%, p = 0.027). Data from exam wrapper response counts can be found in Table 2 . These data indicate that student perceived reasons for missed points (from most to least frequently selected) were careless mistakes, trouble remembering what students studied, changes from correct to incorrect answer, and test anxiety. The most commonly reported study activities (from most to least frequently used) were reading slides, reviewing notes, making study aids, reading the textbook, and group studying. Twenty-seven respondents completed the post-activity survey evaluating their opinions of the exam review and exam wrappers. Twenty of the respondents would like to see this exam review utilized in other courses, and the average rating of how helpful students found wrappers and review sessions was 7 on a 10-point ordered response item. Free text student comments can be found in Table 3 . Table 4 shows the results of the mixed effects model predicting the effect of completion of an exam wrapper on post wrapper exam performance. Using the exam wrapper was associated with a 1.4% point increase on post wrapper exam performance ( p = 0.142) after accounting for other covariates. Among other covariates tested in the model, better performance on Exam 1 was found to predict better overall exam performance ( p < 0.0001). None of the other covariates, including baseline study habits, were predictive of post wrapper exam performance. Table 3 Free text responses to post-activity survey. sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: This study compared students who chose to complete an exam wrapper at least once to those who did not complete any exam wrappers. No attempts were made to compare exam wrapper to standard practice or to a randomly assigned placebo exercise. Additionally, even though exam wrappers and guided self-reflection are inherently metacognitive activities, metacognition was not explicitly measured in this study because authors sought to measure the impact of the metacognitive intervention on objective endpoints of student performance (i.e. exam grades) rather than subjective improvement in metacognition based on participation. Concerns about self-selection bias were partially mitigated by the lack of significant differences between baseline demographics, although values such as motivation and self-efficacy were not evaluated. However, student performance on Exam 1 suggests that those with lower scores are more likely to participate in the exam wrapper than those with higher scores on Exam 1. To account for this difference, Exam 1 performance was introduced as a control variable in the analysis of effectiveness of exam wrappers. The mixed effects model analysis demonstrated in Table 4 shows that the focal independent variable did not significantly affect exam performance, but these findings must be interpreted in the context of the study. A majority of the students in this intervention chose to complete only one wrapper before a single exam. Traditionally in educational research, change of study habits is very difficult to achieve. Therefore, it is possible that students participating strictly during the first exam wrapper (before Exam 2) may have changed their study habits on a temporary basis (i.e. days/weeks) and not for the duration of the course. Despite these chal- lenges, a mixed effects model analysis of the impact of exam wrapper found a 1.4% point increase in performance when accounting for repeated measurements among students and for collected confounders ( p = 0.142). These results suggest that the impact of an exam wrapper should be examined in a more longitudinal context to allow for an assessment of the duration of impact and change of impact over time. This pilot study must also be evaluated in the light of various limitations. Despite efforts to mitigate the self-selection bias by controlling for all measured confounders, it is possible that the study groups differed from each other on other unmeasured con- founders. Additionally, the metacognition presentation delivered to students during orientation may have boosted metacognitive awareness prior to participation in an exam wrapper. We attempted to account for this effect by controlling for scores on the first exam, but it has to be noted that this study does not provide a direct comparison of the intervention against standard practice; it only estimates the effect of students choosing to participate in a metacognition intervention, administered through an exam wrapper. Finally, this single institution study of one course with a small sample size may limit the generalizability of the intervention in a broader programmatic setting. Overall, this activity was generally well-received by the students and may have positively impacted their performance. Based on student feedback, the authors believe that intentional discussion either with the first exam wrapper or in separate small group discussions to orient students to common types of testing errors and resources for effective study habits could be valuable to students. Exam wrappers may just provide a venue to start this rich conversation. Subjectively, researchers involved also felt that exam wrappers shifted the focus of exam reviews and performance from a faculty vs. student discussion to a more constructive discussion with concrete plans and examples for improvement which could alleviate the stress described by Wininger et al. 3 Exam wrappers seem to provide a structured method for metacognitive exercise to assist stud

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Exam wrappers may be a metacognitive tool to be utilized in schools of pharmacy to enhance a culture promoting self-directed and lifelong learning in students. Although not significantly demonstrated in this study, the body of literature regarding exam wrappers indicates they may have potential to positively impact individual student performance in coursework, ultimately leading to greater rates of student success. Additional research beyond this small pilot study is needed to determine the true impact of exam wrappers in pharmacy education.
